name: Glycopyrronium wipes (Qbrexza)
lead: Qbrexza is a prescription cloth containing 2.4% glycopyrronium tosylate, a topical anticholinergic that is wiped onto the underarms once daily to reduce sweating. People use it to keep underarms dry, which in looks terms means fewer visible sweat patches on shirts, less staining and less odor-related concern, and more freedom to wear light colors and fitted clothing.[1][3]

The US FDA approved it in June 2018 for primary axillary hyperhidrosis, initially in people aged 9 and older. A 2019 drug profile describes it as the only alternative to topical antiperspirants specifically approved in children and adolescents 9 and over.[1][3] Wikipedia describes the approval as the first drug developed specifically to reduce excessive sweating.[9]

Phase III trials, a 44-week open-label extension and pharmacokinetic studies describe measurable reductions in sweat output with generally mild to moderate adverse events.[1][5][6] Published case reports also describe pupil dilation in children after accidental transfer of the drug to the eye.[7][8]

paras: Excess underarm sweat shows as wet patches, staining and odor on clothing. People with hyperhidrosis and others who want drier underarms use the cloths as a prescription step beyond over-the-counter antiperspirants.[1][3][11] A T Nation thread on keeping grip dry in summer mentions Qbrexza as something a participant found while searching for hyperhidrosis treatments, showing how it circulates in fitness communities.[10]

The labeled indication is primary axillary hyperhidrosis in adults and children from age 9.[1][3] Hyperhidrosis affects an estimated 4.8 percent of the US population, and severe primary hyperhidrosis is reported to interfere with daily activities and quality of life.[3]

Reviews of the pivotal trials describe improvements in patient-reported severity and in gravimetrically measured sweat production, maintained through long-term treatment of up to 48 weeks.[1][3] The 44-week open-label extension enrolled completers of two 4-week, double-blind, vehicle-controlled phase III trials (NCT02530281 and NCT02530294), in which participants were randomized 2:1 to drug or vehicle once daily.[6] Efficacy measures included sweat weight and the proportion of responders on the Hyperhidrosis Disease Severity Scale.[6]

Glycopyrronium is a peripherally selective antimuscarinic. By blocking acetylcholine receptors on peripheral sweat glands, it reduces the signal that triggers sweating.[3][9] A pharmacokinetic study compared once-daily underarm application (patients aged 9 to 65, five days) with oral glycopyrrolate in healthy adults and analyzed two phase II studies of 0.8 to 3.2% topical drug; its title reports limited systemic exposure with the topical product.[5]

Phase II studies (NCT02016885, NCT02129660) tested topical glycopyrronium at 0.8 to 3.2% versus vehicle in adults with axillary hyperhidrosis and fed a population pharmacokinetic model relating drug levels to efficacy and anticholinergic adverse events.[5]

Two phase III, 4-week, double-blind, vehicle-controlled trials randomized participants 9 years and older 2:1 to the cloth or vehicle; completers could continue in a 44-week open-label extension that monitored adverse events and local skin reactions.[6] Reviews summarize the program as showing reduced sweat production and severity, with most adverse events mild to moderate.[1][3][4]

Case reports in pediatric ophthalmology describe a 2-month-old with one-sided pupil dilation after parental use of the wipes (2019) and a 2022 case series of children with acute mydriasis or anisocoria from exposure to glycopyrronium wipes.[7][8]

Anticholinergic effects such as dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention and constipation are associated with glycopyrronium, and local skin reactions at the application site were assessed in trials.[6][9] Reviews describe adverse events in the trials as mostly mild to moderate.[1] The eye case reports show that drug transferred from hands or from a caregiver to a child's eye can dilate the pupil; the authors suggest clinician familiarity may avoid unnecessary evaluations.[7][8]

Qbrexza is a prescription product marketed for hyperhidrosis. A 2024 Medical Letter review of sofpironium (Sofdra), another topical anticholinergic for axillary hyperhidrosis, shows the class continuing to grow as a prescription option for the condition.[2]

timeline.event: Phase II studies of topical glycopyrronium begin (NCT02016885).[5]
FDA approves topical glycopyrronium tosylate for primary axillary hyperhidrosis.[3][9]
Reviews and a 44-week extension study published; case report of mydriasis in an infant.[1][6][7]
Case series of pediatric mydriasis after wipe exposure.[8]
Sofpironium, another topical anticholinergic, reviewed in The Medical Letter.[2]

lore.intro: Qbrexza appears in fitness forums as a prescription option for sweaty hands and underarms.[10]

claims.claim: A prescription wipe can control sweat for grip and clean-looking clothing
claims.believers: A T Nation participant who searched for hyperhidrosis treatments found Qbrexza and raised it as something that might help with sweat in summer.[10]
claims.experts: The labeled indication is axillary hyperhidrosis, and the trials measured underarm sweat reduction.[1][3] No published trials of palm use exist.

card.summary: Prescription anticholinergic wipes for underarm sweat, FDA-approved in 2018, with case reports of accidental pupil dilation in children.
card.note: Case reports of pupil dilation in children after accidental exposure.

quick.overview:
Qbrexza wipes contain glycopyrronium, an anticholinergic, and are wiped on the underarms to reduce sweating. The FDA approved topical glycopyrronium for primary axillary hyperhidrosis in June 2018.

It is prescription-only.
quick.mechanism: Glycopyrronium blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, reducing the nerve signal that triggers sweat glands.
quick.risks: Anticholinergic effects such as dry mouth and blurred vision are listed for glycopyrronium. Case reports describe pupil dilation in infants and children after accidental exposure.

chain: Wipe applied to dry, clean underarms
Muscarinic receptors on sweat glands are blocked
Less underarm sweat, fewer visible patches and stains
angle.text: Users apply the single-use cloth to the underarms daily to cut sweat production, so shirts stay drier and look cleaner. Studies measured sweat by weight and by patient-reported severity scores.
